pages.x: Sobre nosotros A Madison, Wisconsin web design and development company building dependable technology with care. Quiénes somos Tenshi Systems Engineering is an engineering and technology company. We help organizations plan, build and run the systems they depend on, from custom software and websites to hosting, AI and branding. Creemos que la buena tecnología debe ser fiable, fácil de entender y duradera. Por eso dedicamos tiempo a escuchar, explicamos nuestras decisiones con claridad y seguimos a su lado mucho después del lanzamiento. Nuestro nombre Tenshi means “angel”. For us it is a promise: to look after every project, and every client, with care, from the first conversation to long after launch. Nuestra misión Our mission is to design unique user experiences rapidly with all the cutting edge tools available. Take charge of your business and get started for free today. Nuestra visión A web where every business, from a family shop down the street to a company working across continents, has a website that is well made, honest and quick for everyone who visits it. Nuestra especialidad: la web Ofrecemos nueve servicios, pero la web es donde pasamos la mayor parte del día. Para nosotros, diseño, desarrollo y alojamiento son tres partes del mismo trabajo: un sitio bonito no sirve si es lento, y uno rápido no sirve si se cae. Nos encargamos de los tres para que nada quede en tierra de nadie. Diseño web El diseño empieza por sus visitantes, no por los colores. Estudiamos quiénes son, qué vienen a hacer y qué les frena, y planificamos la estructura de cada página con un mapa del sitio y esquemas. Antes de escribir código, usted recorre un prototipo interactivo en su propio móvil y ordenador, así las ideas se prueban pronto y los cambios cuestan poco. Cada diseño se crea…

pages.x: Web design Nov 6, 2026 · 5 min de lectura Web Forms That Convert: Designing Inquiry and Signup Forms People Actually Finish For many business websites, the form is where everything comes together. All the design, content, and search optimization exist to bring someone to the moment they type their name and press "Send." Yet forms are often treated as an afterthought, assembled quickly from a plugin and never looked at again. When a form is confusing, too long, or quietly broken, interested visitors walk away, and you never learn they were there. Let's look at a form the way your visitors do: before they start, while they fill it in, and after they press the button. Each stage offers practical opportunities to remove friction. Before the First Field: Earning the Click People decide whether to fill out a form before they reach the first field. They are asking themselves two questions: is this worth my time, and can I trust this company with my information? Help them answer yes: Explain what happens next. "We will reply within one business day with a few questions about your project" is far more reassuring than a bare "Submit." State the benefit. Make clear what they will receive, whether that is a quote, a callback, a consultation, or a download. Show the effort upfront. A short form signals respect for their time. If a form must be long, say roughly how long it takes. Place forms where decisions happen. A contact option at the end of each service page catches people at the moment they are ready, rather than sending them hunting for a contact page. Offer alternatives. Some people prefer a phone call, email, or a messaging app. Providing options alongside the form keeps those visitors too. Ask for Less, Ask Clearly Every field is a small request. pages.x: Technology Nov 16, 2026 · 5 min de lectura Website Analytics in Plain English: How to Tell If Your Site Is Doing Its Job A website can look fine and still miss its purpose. Here is how to read the numbers that show whether visitors find you, understand you, and get in touch. A website can look professional, load quickly, and still fall short of the job that matters: helping the right people understand what you offer and take the next step. Analytics will not fix that on its own, but it will show you what is actually happening, instead of what you hope is happening. This guide explains the idea in plain English, names the numbers that usually matter, and suggests a simple monthly habit you can keep. Analytics Is a Record of Behavior, Not a Scorecard Website analytics is a record of how people find your site and what they do while they are there. Typical tools show how many visits you received, which pages were opened, whether someone arrived from a search engine or a link, and whether they used a phone or a computer. That record is useful, but it is not a verdict on your brand, and it is not a sales report. Think of it as a flashlight: it helps you see patterns, not a crystal ball. One well-installed tool, a few clear goals, and a regular look at the results are enough for most small and mid-size businesses. The Numbers That Usually Matter Begin with questions you already have, not with a dashboard full of charts. Are people finding us? Which pages do they read? Do they get as far as contacting us? If a report does not help you answer those questions, you can usually ignore it, including vanity metrics such as raw page-view counts or follower totals that never turn into inquiries. pages.x: Security Nov 11, 2026 · 5 min de lectura Website Security Essentials: A Practical Checklist for Small Businesses It is easy to assume that hackers only go after banks and large corporations. In reality, most attacks on websites are automated. Bots scan the internet around the clock looking for outdated software, weak passwords, and misconfigured servers. They do not care how big your company is; they care whether your site has an open door. A compromised website can show spam to your customers, redirect them to scam pages, leak form submissions, or be flagged by browsers as unsafe. The encouraging news is that a handful of consistent habits prevent the large majority of everyday problems. Think of website security not as one big lock, but as several layers, each one making the next attack harder. Layer One: Encrypt Everything With HTTPS HTTPS encrypts the connection between your visitor's browser and your website, so information like contact form entries and login details cannot be read or altered in transit. It relies on an SSL/TLS certificate installed on your server. What to check: Every page on your site loads with https:// , not just the checkout or contact page. Visitors who type http:// are automatically redirected to the secure version. Your certificate renews automatically. Free certificates from Let's Encrypt, offered by many hosts, typically renew every 90 days, and an expired certificate triggers alarming browser warnings. There is no "mixed content," meaning images or scripts still loading over plain HTTP. Modern browsers label non-HTTPS pages as "Not secure," so this layer protects your reputation as much as your data.
